question:
Malcolm wants to visit Isabella after school today and knows the street where she lives but doesn’t know her house number. She tells him, “My house number has two digits, and exactly three of the following four statements about it are true.”

\((1)\) It is prime.

\((2)\) It is even.

\((3)\) It is divisible by \(7.\)

\((4)\) One of its digits is \(9.\)

This information allows Malcolm to determine Isabella’s house number. What is its units digit?
solution:
Exactly three statements are true, so only one can be false. Start with the prime statement: a two-digit prime cannot be even, because it would have \(2\) as a factor besides \(1\) and itself. It also cannot be divisible by \(7\), because it is larger than \(7\). Thus, if statement \((1)\) were true, statements \((2)\) and \((3)\) would both be false, contradicting the condition.

Therefore statement \((1)\) is false, and statements \((2)\), \((3)\), and \((4)\) are all true. The two-digit even multiples of \(7\) are
\[
14,\ 28,\ 42,\ 56,\ 70,\ 84,\ 98.
\]
This list includes every possibility: the multiples of \(7\) alternate between odd and even, so the even ones occur every \(14\), from \(14\) through \(98\). Only \(98\) contains a digit \(9\). It is composite, even, and divisible by \(7\), so it satisfies exactly the required three statements. Its units digit is \(\boxed{8}\), choice \(\text{D}\).
